common_name: Looking Glass Begonia (Mirror-Leaf Cane Angel Wing Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cane cuttings or nursery starts after all frost danger has passed, siting in bright shade to filtered light; direct midday sun dulls and can scorch the plant's signature reflective foliage.

directions: Grow in bright shade to filtered light in humus-rich, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist, since Looking Glass is more compact and mounding than tree-form cane cultivars like Lucerna and stays a manageable 18-24 inches tall and wide. Its calling card is an almost solid, metallic-silver upper leaf surface threaded with fine olive-green veins, paired with a deep cranberry-red leaf underside that flashes when the wind lifts the foliage. Loose hanging clusters of soft pink flowers appear from late spring through summer above the silvered leaves, though the foliage display, not the bloom, is the main event with this cultivar. Keep humidity moderate to high and water at the soil line rather than overhead to prevent leaf spot on the glossy leaf surface.
sources: American Begonia Society cane-type begonia references

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and grow on in a large hanging basket or tall container, siting in bright shade after all frost danger has passed; give the scandent stems room to cascade well below the pot rim.

directions: Grow in a large hanging basket or tall container in bright to moderate shade, since Withlacoochee is a scandent (trailing/climbing) hybrid of Begonia thelmae and Begonia peruviana rather than an upright cane type. Small, fuzzy-textured leaves in bronze, green, and red tones clothe long, wiry, cascading stems, and clusters of pearly white flowers appear intermittently nearly year-round in warm climates, earning it the nickname Bridalveil Begonia. Unlike the stiff, self-supporting canes of Lucerna or Sophie Cecile, this cultivar's stems trail and weave, making it best suited to elevated planters, tall stands, or hanging displays rather than garden beds. Keep the potting mix evenly moist but never soggy and provide a large enough container, since crowded roots slow its otherwise vigorous trailing growth.
sources: American Begonia Society cultivar registration records

common_name: Cocktail Gin Begonia (Bronze-Leaf Rose-Pink Wax Begonia)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost since Cocktail series begonias grow slowly from seed; transplant outdoors only after frost danger has fully passed. Gin is the rose-pink-flowered, bronze-leaved member of the series.

directions: Sow dust-fine seed on the surface of moist, sterile starting mix under bright light without covering, since germination depends on light exposure and seedlings take many weeks to reach transplant size. Gin carries the same glossy bronze-maroon foliage as its Cocktail-series siblings but is distinguished by loose clusters of soft rose-pink flowers rather than Vodka's scarlet or Whiskey's white. The tight, uniform mound needs no deadheading and blooms continuously from spring through the first hard frost, and the dark leaf pigment lets it tolerate brighter light than green-leaved wax begonias without scorching. Use it as edging or in mixed containers where a softer pink tone is wanted alongside bolder Cocktail-series colors.
sources: Benary — Begonia semperflorens F1 Cocktail series product page

common_name: Ambassador Scarlet Begonia (Green-Leaf Bedding Wax Begonia)

planting.note: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost using fine pelleted seed, then transplant outdoors after frost danger passes; Ambassador tolerates more direct sun than shade-only wax begonias, so it can go in beds with morning-to-midday exposure.

directions: Start seed indoors under bright light on a heat mat, then transplant into moist, well-drained bedding soil once frost danger has passed. Ambassador Scarlet is a green-leaf semperflorens selection bred for mass bedding production, bearing large scarlet flowers with contrasting yellow center stamens over glossy true-green foliage rather than the bronze leaf color seen in the Cocktail series. Its clean, compact, heavily basal-branched mound holds up in full sun to partial shade and keeps flowering steadily through summer heat and humidity, making it a common substitute for shade-impatiens plantings where downy mildew has been a problem. Feed lightly through the season and keep soil evenly moist for the most continuous bloom.
sources: Harris Seeds product listing: Begonia Ambassador Scarlet F1

common_name: Illumination Apricot Shades Begonia (Trailing Multi-Tone Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Start tubers indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or set out started nursery plants after frost danger has passed, in a hanging basket or elevated container in partial sun to bright shade.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or window box filled with rich, evenly moist, well-drained potting mix, giving it a bit more light than deep-shade tuberous types since Apricot Shades tolerates partial sun and even attracts hummingbirds to its blooms. Unlike solid-color trailing selections in the Illumination series, Apricot Shades produces fully double flowers that blend salmon, apricot, coral, and soft yellow within the same cluster, creating a shifting, multi-tone cascade along the trailing stems rather than a single flat color. The trailing habit needs no staking, but the heavy flower load benefits from regular light feeding and a consistently moist root zone. Where winters are too cold to leave tubers in the ground, lift and store them dry over winter for replanting the following spring.
sources: Proven Winners — Illumination Apricot Shades Tuberous Begonia
Benary — Begonia tuberhybrida F1 Illumination series product page

common_name: Nonstop Yellow Begonia (Compact Upright Golden-Yellow Tuberous Begonia)

planting.note: Start tubers indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or plant started nursery plants outdoors after frost danger has passed, in moist, well-drained soil or containers in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or containers in partial to full shade. Nonstop Yellow produces fully double, rose-form flowers up to 4 inches across in a clear, bright yellow, packed with tightly layered petals that resemble a miniature rose rather than the simple open form of species begonias. Like its Nonstop-series relatives such as Nonstop Fire and Nonstop Rose, it forms a dense, compact mound that blooms continuously from late spring until frost without deadheading, but its lighter flower color makes it useful for brightening shaded beds and containers where warm reds and oranges dominate the rest of the series. It also tolerates somewhat more sun than many shade begonias, giving extra placement flexibility in beds with a few hours of morning light. Where winters are too cold to leave tubers in the ground, lift and store them dry over winter for replanting the following spring.
sources: Proven Winners — Nonstop Yellow Tuberous Begonia
